solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A January snow melts — slime! — was salt spread out? He's served his time

indicators.note: spread out tells us the letters of the first phrase are scattered and rearranged, once the second phrase's letters are taken away

parts.note: the letters of these four words form the pool
these letters are the ones removed from the pool

explanation.surface: A winter scene: January snow turning to slush after someone has gritted the road, rounded off with a craftsman's credentials.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: take WAS SALT out of A JANUARY SNOW MELTS and 'spread out' what remains. 'slime!' is a rhyming flourish: every clue in this puzzle is a rhyming couplet naming the months in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who has completed an apprenticeship and works for wages has served his time.

clue.text: It'll raise flag flown by ship

definitions.meaning: a device for lifting heavy things such as a car
a small national flag flown at a vessel's bow

explanation.surface: A sailor hoisting a flag above the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a lifting device used under a car and a small flag flown at a ship's bow, as in the Union flag.

clue.text: Mid-July do mischief. Hoot!

indicators.note: do is short for ditto, meaning the same again, so the previous piece is repeated
Mid takes the central letters of July

parts.note: Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin

explanation.surface: A midsummer prank, met with a cry of laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a verb but is ditto, repeating UL.
explanation.definitionFit: To howl or wail loudly, as an owl hoots.

clue.text: Kind honour, life in birthday-suit

parts.note: kind as a noun means sort or character
to honour a deity is to revere or adore it

explanation.surface: A tribute to the gentle naturist lifestyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'birthday-suit' is a jokey term for nakedness.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturism, living unclothed in the open air, is described here through reverence for the natural world.

clue.text: City month, August? Not out? Must seek recreation. Sailing? Just!

indicators.note: Not shows that the following words are absent from the anagram
re-creation suggests making again, so the remaining letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of these two words go into the pool
this word's letters join the pool
these letters are removed from the pool
these letters are removed from the pool too

explanation.surface: An office worker in August needs a break: sailing, just about.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: remove OUT and MUST from CITY MONTH AUGUST and remix the rest. 'Just!' is a rhyming flourish.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a boat out on the water as a sport or pastime is this pursuit.

clue.text: Trained doula how to shout out 'Hup!'

indicators.note: trained suggests reshaping something, so the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A birth attendant teaching a mother to call out during labour.
explanation.walkthrough: A doula is a non-medical birth companion. 'Hup!' completes the rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking in an audible voice rather than silently is the way any shout is made.

clue.text: Censure a Major …

definitions.meaning: to criticise harshly, as a newspaper might a poor performance
a Grand ... event, one of tennis's four major tournaments

explanation.surface: A political attack on a prime minister: censuring John Major.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a Major' looks like the former prime minister John Major, but it is one of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments, which lead into the next clue about Margaret Court.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan or criticise savagely is to slam; a tennis major is a Grand Slam tournament.

clue.text: I love Scots starters — slice eel up

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the letters read from bottom to top, backwards
slice suggests cutting into the eel, letting the other piece sit within it

parts.note: meze is a selection of small dishes served as starters

explanation.surface: Someone declaring a fondness for Scottish appetisers, such as sliced eel.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scots expression of affection, roughly meaning dear is to me, used as an exclamation of love.

clue.text: Mid-September Saturday is as put another way transition.

indicators.note: put another way means said differently, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the middle of September is its central three letters, the fourth to sixth

explanation.surface: A diary entry for a Saturday in mid-September, rephrased.
explanation.definitionFit: The spread or shift of a disease from one site to another, and in rhetoric a passing over; a change of state.

clue.text: … Roll or cut grass for Margaret; that's where she showed class

definitions.text: grass for Margaret; that's where she showed class

indicators.note: to roll something is to turn it over, so these letters are tumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Mowing or rolling the lawn where a great tennis champion once played.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Court was an Australian tennis champion, many times a winner on grass at Wimbledon; her surname is also the playing area itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A grass court is where tennis is played, and Court is the surname of the champion Margaret, so both senses lie in the phrase.

clue.text: Wet February 1st score out lines.

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged
the 1st of February is taken as its first letter only

explanation.surface: A rainy start to February, with someone deleting lines from a musical score.
explanation.definitionFit: Crow's feet are the fine wrinkles that fan out from the corners of the eyes, i.e. facial lines.

clue.text: Rock band is given a ten (of sorts) for that's how things were then

parts.note: Status Quo is a long-running British rock group

indicators.note: of sorts means in a rough form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rock band receiving a rating of ten out of ten.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin phrase means the state of affairs as it existed before, so the earlier situation.

clue.text: Pops swear tea trade's up the spout

indicators.note: up the spout means ruined or broken, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter; the word gives TRADE

explanation.surface: Father curses because the tea trade has collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pops' looks like a father or several fathers, but it is plural fizzy drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is fizzy soft drink, and carbonated waters are the bubbly kind.

clue.text: To smash to smithereens stein can be the aim of one who goes TT

definitions.text: the aim of one who goes TT

indicators.note: smashing to smithereens breaks something into pieces, so these letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A teetotaller breaking a beer mug to keep away from drink.
explanation.walkthrough: TT means teetotal.
explanation.definitionFit: Teetotallers refrain from alcohol completely; refraining is their goal.

clue.text: We beings laboured for a crust

indicators.note: laboured suggests strain and reworking, signalling an anagram of the preceding words

explanation.surface: People toiling to earn their daily bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a crust' looks like a living earned, but it is the filmy deposit found in old port wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A filmy crust of tartar that forms in long-kept port wine is known by this name.

clue.text: Spain and UK are bust I've sussed

parts.note: E is the international vehicle registration letter for Spain (España)

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A financial commentator declares that both Spain and Britain are bankrupt, claiming to have worked it out.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation of Archimedes on discovering something, meaning 'I have found it', so a cry of having worked it out.

clue.text: October, Aussie. Pull that ring! Brew guaranteed to give most zing

indicators.note: Pull means take out, so the ring's letter is removed from the pool
brewing stirs things together, so the remaining letters are mixed

parts.note: the letters of this word join the pool
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: An Australian in October pulls a ring-pull on a beer can and enjoys the zingy drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Saucy means lively and piquant, and the superlative gives the most piquancy.

clue.text: The Terriers March accepted spice

parts.note: the Territorial Army (TA), Britain's volunteer reserve, was nicknamed the Terriers
A is a standard abbreviation for accepted, as on a bill of exchange

explanation.surface: A volunteer regiment's march is agreed, with a hint of seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Terriers' look like dogs or a football team, but they are the Territorial Army, Britain's part-time reserve force.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamara is an Italian blend of seasonings, such as cinnamon, cloves and coriander, used in cooking.

clue.text: November 5th; in river, me, figure of Guy, say, mimicry

indicators.note: 5th selects the fifth letter of November
in shows one piece placed inside the other

parts.note: the Isis is the name given to the Thames at Oxford

explanation.surface: Bonfire night, when an effigy of Guy Fawkes stands as a copy of the real man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figure of Guy, say' joins the definition in spirit: the Guy burned on November 5th is an imitation of Fawkes.
explanation.definitionFit: A term for imitation or representation, especially of reality in art, as an effigy imitates a person.

clue.text: Change a quid — Irish one? Grog with ice?

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its form, so these letters are reshuffled

parts.note: the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: Someone at a bar asks for change of a pound, perhaps an Irish one, before ordering a cold drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A quid is British slang for a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: A rum cocktail with lime and sugar, often served over crushed ice; grog loosely means alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Chips will half cooked still go down somehow in this county town

indicators.note: cooked means altered or prepared, so the letters are rearranged
half takes the first half of the word will

explanation.surface: Fried food is still eaten somehow in a provincial town.
explanation.walkthrough: Ipswich is the county town of Suffolk.
explanation.definitionFit: The main administrative town of the county of Suffolk, in eastern England.

clue.text: April's first English paeony's much abloom. All buttercups are such

indicators.note: abloom suggests opening out into new forms, so the letters are rearranged
first takes just the opening letter of the word April's

parts.note: here the possessive S of paeony's is kept as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: A spring gardening note: in April the peonies are flowering profusely, and the buttercups are in the same state.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of paeony's counts here, unlike most possessives. The botanical classification in the definition belongs to the old system that grouped water-lilies with buttercups.
explanation.definitionFit: This botanical adjective means belonging to the water-lily family, once classed alongside the buttercups in older plant systems.

clue.text: Almost December. Aunt's suspect but Dec's lost fluid to inject

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious or untrustworthy, so the letters are reworked
lost shows these letters being removed from the pool
Almost drops the final letter of December

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter
taken as written
DEC is the abbreviation for December; the 's adds nothing

explanation.surface: An aunt's health is in doubt in late December, needing a medical injection.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: take BUT and DEC from DECEMBE (December, 'almost') plus AUNT and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical procedure in which liquid is injected into the rectum, or the liquid itself.

clue.text: This artificial creature falls in Coleridge epic (with apols.)

indicators.note: in shows the letters are found inside the following words

explanation.surface: An apology for referring to a monstrous creature in a Coleridge epic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket apologises because Coleridge wrote no epic.
explanation.definitionFit: A laboratory-made goat-sheep chimera, produced by combining embryos of the two species.

clue.text: May nozzle spoil old epic seen?

indicators.note: to spoil something is to mar it, so these letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A worried question whether a spout might ruin a screening of an old film epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' is the month that this couplet must name and plays no part in the wordplay: the anagram is of O and EPIC SEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A fitting at the end of a hose or pipe through which liquid comes out is a nozzle.

clue.text: Church body split by one that's green

indicators.note: split by shows the first part being parted to let the next piece sit inside

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church building
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: A congregation divided by one inexperienced member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church body' looks like a governing assembly, but it is the central part of the building.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means inexperienced and easily fooled, which is innocent and unsophisticated.

clue.text: June finally as English is as being free from any tizz

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of June

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An Englishman in June stays calm and unflustered.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfort and freedom from worry or agitation; a tizz is a state of nervous fluster.

clue.text: Face the bowling; fox the slip — great craft!

parts.note: in cricket, to face the bowling is to bat

indicators.note: fox means confuse, so these letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A cricketing scene: a batsman at the crease outwits the fielder at slip.
explanation.walkthrough: Slip is a close-catching fielding position behind the batsman in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavily armed warship is a great vessel, and craft means boats or ships.
